peer_matches.query_passage: Kestrel's gross margin erosion is mainly a procurement problem. The company buys edible oil and potatoes on the spot market, so when commodity prices surged it absorbed the full increase without any contractual protection. Retailer power made things worse: large supermarket chains extracted bigger promotional allowances while Kestrel kept its list prices flat for fear of losing shelf space. Selling directly to consumers would give Kestrel valuable first-party data and higher realised prices per pack. However, the economics of delivering low-value snack orders are poor, and building a digital brand requires sustained marketing spend that the current margin cannot support. Modern trade offers scale and visibility immediately. We therefore recommend strengthening the modern-trade relationship through joint business plans rather than launching a separate online channel now. Year one should focus on procurement: Kestrel should negotiate annual price agreements with oil refiners and start a contract farming programme with potato growers in Maharashtra. Year two should focus on simplification: the company should remove the slowest-selling variants and redirect marketing money to its five best-selling brands. Key metrics include gross margin, procurement cost per kilogram, revenue per variant and retailer fill rate. The biggest risk is that farmers break contracts when spot prices rise above the agreed price.
